text: A product launch, a flash sale, a Black Friday weekend — these are spikes you already know are coming, on a specific date, often with an estimable magnitude. That makes this the most plannable failure mode in all of capacity engineering. It also still catches teams constantly, almost always because the plan existed only as an assumption instead of an actual written, owned, dated plan.

A real pre-scaling plan works backward from the event date. Estimate the spike's magnitude from the best signal you have — last year's equivalent event, marketing's projected reach — and err high, the same headroom discipline as routine forecasting. Pre-provision capacity accounting for lead time, so quota increases and replica scaling actually clear before the event. And load test against this event's exact expected mix, not a generic test, because a launch-day flash of traffic behaves nothing like steady-state load.

Every step gets a name and a date attached to it, worked backward from the event: the quota increase requested three weeks out, autoscaling pre-warmed two weeks out, read replicas scaled ten days out, the event-specific load test run five days out, dashboards and a staffed war room ready the day before. None of that happens by itself just because everyone agrees it's important.

The goal is for the first sign of trouble to come from a dashboard, not a customer. That means event-specific dashboards, alert thresholds tuned for expected spike traffic, a staffed escalation path, and kill switches ready to shed non-essential load — a recommendation engine, background jobs — all built and tested before the event starts, not improvised while it's already underway.

A complete plan doesn't stop at surviving the peak. It includes scaling back down once the event ends, so provisioned capacity doesn't keep running up cost indefinitely, and a rollback path written in advance for any single pre-scaling action that turns out to cause its own problem — the same calm-in-advance discipline as a disaster recovery runbook, figured out ahead of time instead of invented under pressure.

That closes out capacity planning and performance engineering: forecast from real data, test with realistic traffic, treat performance as an ongoing discipline, and plan the spikes you can see coming with the same rigor. Next, this course turns to on-call and operational excellence — keeping the people running all of this sustainable over the long run.
